articles.title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
articles.summary: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.
articles.body:
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.

The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule . She denies the charges.

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.

Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.

The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.

But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.

Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.

Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.

But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.

Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.

The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title: A mother and her three children were stranded in Panama for 33 days after Air Canada raised concerns about their valid Canadian visas; a Federal Court ordered the airline to pay C$4,129
articles.summary: A mother and her three children arrived at an airport in Panama in August 2017, ready to board a flight to Toronto.
articles.body: A mother and her three children arrived at an airport in Panama in August 2017, ready to board a flight to Toronto. They had valid Canadian visas, but questions raised by Air Canada staff about their travel plans led to the documents being cancelled before they could fly. The family ended up spending another 33 days in Panama while trying to get the visas reinstated. The dispute eventually reached Canada's Federal Court, which examined the airline's role in the events and the expenses the family had incurred. In its April 2025 judgment in Mejias Turmero v. Air Canada and Attorney General of Canada, 2025 FC 673, the court ordered Air Canada to pay C$4,129.04.How Air Canada's check-in questions led to visa troubleNazarelys Paula Mejias Turmero was travelling to Toronto with her three children on 4 August 2017. The family had booked one-way seats on Air Canada flight AC 1949 from Panama City. They already had valid Canadian visas and were hoping to join Ms. Mejias's husband, who was studying in Toronto.Questions came up when they reached the check-in desk. An Air Canada employee wanted to know more about their journey. Ms. Mejias explained that it was their first trip to Canada and that her husband planned to apply for a post-graduation work permit after finishing his studies. The employee said he would need to speak to immigration officials before proceeding.The conversation was then taken further by his supervisor, Ms. Corrales, who contacted a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) liaison officer in Panama. She raised concerns about the family's luggage and one-way tickets, as well as the number of people leaving Venezuela. Her concern was that the family might not leave Canada when they were supposed to. However, the explanation about the husband's plans to apply for a work permit was not included in the information passed on to immigration officials.However, the court later observed that the supervisor had not passed on an important part of the explanation given by Ms. Mejias: her husband's plans to apply for a work permit after completing his studies.A phone call led to the cancellation of their Canadian visasThe information provided by the airline supervisor was passed through the immigration channel to an official based in Mexico City, identified as Mr. Francis. The official cancelled the family's Canadian visas on the same day, leaving the mother and her children unable to continue their journey.The family was in Panama without the documents needed to board their booked flight to Canada. They had to find a way to have the visas restored before they could travel.On 28 August 2017, a lawyer representing Ms. Mejias contacted Mr. Francis and explained the circumstances surrounding her husband's studies and his intended work permit application. Following this communication, the visas were issued again. Air Canada also arranged new flights for the family without charging them for the rebooking.The passengers eventually arrived in Toronto on 6 September 2017, 33 days after their original departure date. During that period, Ms. Mejias and her children had to meet their accommodation and day-to-day living expenses in Panama.Mother took Air Canada to the Federal CourtMs. Mejias eventually took the matter to Canada's Federal Court. Representing herself, she sought USD 4,520.13 from Air Canada, claiming the money she and her children had spent because they could not travel as planned. Her claim was brought under Article 19 of the Montreal Convention, which covers losses caused by delays in international air travel.She also named the Attorney General of Canada in a separate claim, accusing immigration authorities of negligence and seeking public law damages. In court, she questioned Air Canada's account of the airport exchange. The airline's own records did not show that the male check-in agent had entered the family's visa details into its system. Ms. Corrales, the supervisor who contacted the CBSA, also admitted she had not heard the conversation herself. She had no first-hand knowledge of the answers Ms. Mejias had given at the counter.That left an important gap in the airline's version of events. The explanation about her husband's plans to apply for a work permit had not been passed on to the immigration official who cancelled the family's visas.What Air Canada argued in its defenceThe airline disputed the interpretation of Article 19 of the Montreal Convention. Its position was that it was required to demonstrate that it had taken reasonable steps to prevent the damage caused by the delay, rather than prove that it had done everything possible to avoid the delay itself. Air Canada also referred to its obligations concerning passengers travelling to Canada without the necessary documentation. It maintained that its employees had acted within the scope of those responsibilities when they raised concerns with immigration authorities.The airline questioned the need to call the male check-in employee as a witness, arguing that the supervisor's evidence was sufficient. Both Air Canada and the federal government also challenged the expenses claimed by Ms. Mejias, raising the issue of whether she had taken reasonable steps to limit her losses.During the proceedings, the possibility of returning to Venezuela rather than remaining in Panama was raised. The defence suggested that the family could have made that journey for approximately USD 240. It also argued that some of the claimed food and living expenses would have been incurred regardless of where the family stayed.Why the court held the airline responsibleThe Federal Court did not accept Air Canada's interpretation of the Montreal Convention. In its examination of the applicable legal principles, it concluded that the airline had to establish that it had taken all reasonable measures to avoid the delay, not simply that it had tried to limit the financial consequences once the delay occurred.The court also distinguished the case from situations in which passengers are refused boarding because they do not possess valid travel documents. Ms. Mejias and her children had valid visas when they arrived at the airport. The court found that their cancellation followed a sequence of events initiated by Air Canada's employees.The airline's evidence presented further difficulties. The male employee who had first questioned Ms. Mejias was not called to testify, and no explanation was provided for his absence. The court also found problems with the reliability of Ms. Corrales's account. Her failure to communicate the husband's work permit plans to the CBSA liaison officer was another point considered by the judge. The court drew an adverse inference from the airline's decision not to produce the original employee as a witness, concluding that his testimony would likely not have supported its position. As a result, Air Canada failed to establish the defence available to it under Article 19.Why the court rejected Air Canada's argument about returning to VenezuelaThe court also considered the airline's argument that Ms. Mejias should have returned to Venezuela instead of remaining in Panama while the visa issue was being resolved. It rejected the suggestion that her decision amounted to a failure to mitigate the family's losses. When they arrived at the airport on 4 August, there was no way for the family to know that the problem would keep them away from Canada for more than a month.Their decision to stay in Panama while attempting to understand the cancellation and secure the return of their visas was considered reasonable in the circumstances. The court did not find that they had acted unreasonably by choosing to resolve the matter rather than immediately travel back to Venezuela.Which expenses were included in the compensationThe hotel was the biggest expense the court accepted. Ms. Mejias had submitted a bill for USD 2,301.10, and the full amount was allowed. Food bills and other day-to-day expenses were also included where receipts showed what the family had spent during their extended stay in Panama.The pharmacy bill was treated differently. Ms. Mejias had claimed USD 311.36, but her children had chickenpox during the same period. The court could not establish how much of the medical spending was linked to the delay caused by Air Canada, so it did not allow the full amount.There was also USD 925.50 in expenses for which Ms. Mejias had no receipts. Those claims were turned down. The court was not prepared to award money on the basis of estimates alone.Air Canada ordered to pay C$4,129.04In its 2025 judgment, Mejias Turmero v. Air Canada and Attorney General of Canada, 2025 FC 673, the Federal Court ordered Air Canada to pay Ms. Mejias C$4,129.04. The amount represented USD 3,283.27 converted at an exchange rate of 1.2576.The award also included interest at 2% from 20 August 2017, followed by interest at 4.75% after the judgment. The question of legal costs was left open for further submissions.Disclaimer: This article is based on the judgment delivered by the Federal Court of Canada in Mejias Turmero v. Air Canada and Attorney General of Canada, 2025 FC 673, and other publicly available information. The Times of India has not independently verified the circumstances beyond the details available in the cited court records.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott donates another $12.5 million to Georgia nonprofits, helping students pursue higher education, with one organisation receiving its second $8 million gift
articles.summary: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott has donated another $12.5 million to two Georgia-based nonprofits working to expand access to
articles.body: Jeff Bezos' ex-wife and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott has donated another $12.5 million to two Georgia-based nonprofits working to expand access to higher education. The contributions include an $8 million grant to Achieve Atlanta, marking Scott's second donation of the same amount to the organisation, and $4.5 million to the Jeannette Rankin Foundation, which supports women pursuing education later in life. The latest contributions are part of Scott's philanthropic initiative, Yield Giving, through which she has distributed billions of dollars to nonprofit organisations across the US. While Achieve Atlanta focuses on helping students access and complete post-secondary education, the foundation provides financial assistance to women facing economic barriers to higher education.MacKenzie Scott gives Achieve Atlanta another $8 millionAchieve Atlanta announced that it had received another $8 million contribution from Scott, following her first donation of the same amount in 2022. The organisation works with Atlanta Public Schools, Fulton County Schools and post-secondary institutions to help students afford college, remain enrolled and complete their education.It currently supports more than 8,700 students, known as Scholars, across Atlanta Public Schools and six high schools in Fulton County. Its programmes include assistance with selecting colleges, completing applications, academic guidance, social and emotional support, and finding their first jobs.Since 2015, Achieve Atlanta has distributed more than $75 million in scholarships. The organisation said Scott's latest contribution would help extend its work and strengthen opportunities for students pursuing higher education.Dr Cheryl Watson-Harris, president and executive director of Achieve Atlanta, said the donation recognised the determination and aspirations of its students. She added that the contribution affirmed the organisation's belief that talent is equally distributed, even when opportunities are not.Jeannette Rankin Foundation receives its largest-ever donationThe second recipient, the Athens-based Jeannette Rankin Foundation, received $4.5 million, marking the largest single donation in its 50-year history.Founded in 1976, the organisation supports women facing financial barriers to higher education. Its programmes provide grants and assistance to women pursuing vocational and technical qualifications, associate degrees and their first bachelor's degrees.The foundation currently supports more than 400 scholars annually, compared with 86 a few years ago. Its support is designed to help women overcome financial obstacles that could otherwise prevent them from continuing their education.Chief executive Karen Sterk said the donation would give the foundation an opportunity to expand its reach. She also highlighted that more than one million women across the US could potentially benefit from its support.According to the foundation, Scott's contribution was unsolicited and followed independent research conducted by her team. The organisation said the funding would help shape its work over the next 50 years.What is MacKenzie Scott's Yield Giving initiative?The latest contributions were made through Yield Giving, Scott's philanthropic initiative, which supports nonprofit organisations working across different sectors in the US.Unlike conventional grant-making programmes that require organisations to submit applications and follow specific spending conditions, Scott is known for making unsolicited donations and providing recipients with flexibility over how they use the funds. The latest donations have also been reported as unrestricted, allowing the organisations to direct the money towards their respective missions.Through Yield Giving, Scott has supported organisations working in education, economic mobility, racial equity, healthcare and other areas. Her approach has drawn attention for providing large contributions without requiring recipients to compete through conventional funding applications.MacKenzie Scott's philanthropy following her divorce from Jeff BezosScott, an American novelist and philanthropist, was married to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos for 25 years before the couple announced their divorce in 2019. As part of their divorce settlement, she received a 4% stake in Amazon, worth approximately $36 billion at the time.Following the divorce, she pledged to give away the majority of her wealth to charitable causes during her lifetime and signed the Giving Pledge in May 2019.Her philanthropic contributions have since reached billions of dollars, supporting thousands of organisations across the US. Her donations have included educational institutions, community organisations and nonprofits working to improve opportunities for disadvantaged communities.With the latest $12.5 million contribution to the two Georgia nonprofits, Scott continues her efforts to support organisations working to expand educational access and help more people pursue higher education.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2026, a Montana family put 110 acres once slated for eight homes under a conservation easement, adding to the 655 acres they protected near Whitefish in 2022
articles.summary: In a remarkable conservation effort, Doug and Carolyn Kohrs have added 110 acres of land along the Stillwater River to a conservation easement, preserving it from development and protecting wildlife habitats in Montana.
articles.body: Few things hurt as much as watching a favourite green spot turn into rows of new homes. In Montana, one family decided on a very different ending for land they loved. In early January 2026, Doug and Carolyn Kohrs placed 110 acres on the Stillwater River under the conservation easement, the Daily Inter Lake reported. Before the couple acquired the land, it was slated for an eight-home subdivision. That adds to the 655 acres the Kohrs protected near Whitefish in 2022. Together, the two parcels make up one larger block of protected land, and Doug Kohrs said he and his wife were excited to add to it.What a conservation easement actually doesThe conservation easement is basically a deal between the landowner and the land trust. Land trusts are organisations that work with landowners to protect the land. The owner keeps the land but gives up some of the rights to develop it. Here, the terms bar the land from being subdivided or developed. Farming can still continue, and the land remains a working ground as well as a wild one at the same time. The easement agreement is also perpetual, which means every future owner will have to abide by the same conditions. This is important because a promise made by one family binds all future owners of the land.Why this stretch of river matters so muchThe new land sits on the Stillwater River in Flathead County, west of Whitefish. Flathead Land Trust, the nonprofit that works with the family, says the easement adds a quarter mile of riverfront and extends the protected stretch to more than three miles in total. The land connects to the 1,560-acre Kuhns Wildlife Management Area and borders an undeveloped habitat block of nearly 5,000 acres that includes state and federal forest. The trust reports that grizzly and black bears have been documented using the property as a travel corridor. Game cameras on the site have also captured mountain lions, wolves, bobcats, coyotes and foxes. Elk calves and deer fawns have also been recorded. The river is home to threatened bull trout and Westslope cutthroat trout. The Kohrs have seen 95 species of birds there themselves. These are records from the family and the land trust, not from an independent survey.What research says about wildlife corridorsWildlife corridors are strips of habitat where animals can move between larger wilderness areas. One way to think of them is like highways for wildlife. When habitats are broken into pieces, animals have more difficulty moving around. A 2023 paper published in Biological Conservation used GPS-collar data on 65 grizzly bears to create models of their likely travel paths. The study indicates that the routes were mainly linked to mountainous regions. Next were rivers and streams in open valleys. The authors also stress that there are fragmented populations of grizzly bears in the continental US. Connecting them together is one of the goals of conservation. While the research didn't mention the Kohrs’ land, it helps explain why this protected stretch of river matters to bears on the move.The Kohrs long-term conservation effortThe Kohrs began buying land in the area in 2005, according to the land trust. In 2022, they conserved 655 acres, then added another 110 acres in 2026. Doug Kohrs said that wildlife corridors are important for the valley's many animals since developments are encroaching on their habitat. It's a worry familiar to most fast-growing towns. One easement might not solve all the problems of Flathead Valley wildlife, but it keeps this stretch of river from being chopped up into house plots. That can help the animals that depend on it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Washington’s King County bought 475 acres of forestland for $6.75 million in its biggest land deal by acreage in over 20 years, permanently protecting about seven miles of popular woodland trails
articles.summary: A forest is more than just a stretch of trees.
articles.body: A forest is more than just a stretch of trees. It is a habitat for wildlife, a natural resource for surrounding communities and, sometimes, a place where people find a little distance from the noise of everyday life. Recognising the importance of preserving such spaces, King County in Washington has purchased 475 acres of forestland in the Snoqualmie Valley for $6.75 million. The acquisition will permanently protect approximately seven miles of popular backcountry trails, ensuring that the woodland remains a forest rather than being opened up for development.According to an announcement published by the King County Department of Natural Resources and Parks on November 16, 2026, the acquisition marks the county's largest land purchase by acreage in more than 20 years. The county secured the property, known as Tokul West, through a successful auction bid using funds from its Conservation Futures Program and King County Parks Levy. The purchase will not require any additional tax revenue. The property is located near Fall City and forms part of the larger forestland area known as Twin Peaks Forest.As Jesse Cunningham, Interim Director of the Evergreen Mountain Bike Alliance, said, “Protecting a large portion of the Tokul West trail network is a significant win for thousands of riders and outdoor enthusiasts.” Why the forestland needed protectionThe newly acquired property is part of the Tokul trail network, a popular outdoor recreation destination in the Snoqualmie Valley. Its trails are used by mountain bikers, horseback riders and hikers, and connect with the wider Snoqualmie Valley Trail system.Until the acquisition, the trail network was operated by a private company that charged visitors entry fees. The sale of the forestland had raised concerns among outdoor enthusiasts about whether the trails would remain accessible and whether the surrounding woodland could eventually be developed.By purchasing the land, King County has secured a significant portion of the trail network and placed it under public ownership. King County Parks will manage the property, overseeing trail safety and accessibility standards.County Executive Girmay Zahilay described the acquisition as a major step towards long-term land conservation.“Purchasing 475 acres of contiguous forestland in the Snoqualmie Valley is a generational achievement for land conservation in King County,” Zahilay said. He added that the purchase would ensure the land remains forested while preserving access to popular backcountry trails without requiring additional tax revenue.Protecting forests while directing urban developmentThe acquisition is also connected to King County's broader approach to balancing conservation with urban growth. Through its Transfer of Development Rights programme, the county plans to sell development rights associated with the newly protected forestland to developers in designated urban areas.Under this system, developers can purchase credits that allow them to add housing units or increase building height in certain urban locations, including downtown Seattle. The idea is to direct development towards areas suited for higher density while keeping rural and environmentally significant land protected.King County officials say the programme has helped preserve more than 150,000 acres since its establishment in 1998. The latest acquisition also contributes to the county's Land Conservation Initiative, which aims to protect 65,000 acres of open space within a generation.The purchase has also received support from the Snoqualmie Tribe, which recognises the area's cultural and environmental importance. The forestland lies within the Snoqualmie River Watershed and forms part of the Tribe's ancestral landscape.“The Snoqualmie Tribe applauds King County in taking a step to help protect more forestlands from development,” said Tribal Chairman Robert de los Angeles, while encouraging visitors to respect the cultural significance of Snoqualmie ancestral lands.While the acquisition secures only a portion of the larger Twin Peaks Forest, it represents a significant step towards protecting the region's woodland and recreational spaces. For the people who hike, cycle or ride through these trails, it also means that a familiar stretch of forest will remain part of the landscape for generations to come.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 5.5-mile levee separated 965 acres of Washington’s Steigerwald Refuge from the Columbia River from the 1960s; a $32 million project removed 2.2 miles of it in 2021
articles.summary: Discover how a $32 million restoration project at Washington's Steigerwald Refuge removed an old levee, enhancing floodplain habitat for young salmon while protecting local communities.
articles.body: Rivers are meant to spill over their banks every now and then. That's how they feed the land around them. For decades, a stretch of the Columbia River in Washington state couldn't. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a levee at Steigerwald Lake National Wildlife Refuge blocked Gibbons Creek from draining into the river naturally. It also cut fish off from the floodplain habitat that young salmon need. A massive restoration project was created to change that.A levee that remained for decadesA levee is a bank of earth built to hold water back. This one stretched for 5.5 miles. From the 1960s till 2021, it separated the Columbia River from 965 acres of its natural floodplain. A floodplain is the relatively flat, low-lying area of land adjacent to a river that floods during wet seasons. While the levee was supposed to reduce flooding risks, it ended up creating some problems as well. The Fish and Wildlife Service says Gibbons Creek could not drain naturally, thus causing floods on both public and private land surrounding the refuge.Why young salmon need floodplains Floodplains provide important habitat for wildlife. Young salmon need shallow, slow-moving water to rest during their long, tough journey to the sea. The Fish and Wildlife Service explains that the old levee blocked fish passage and cut fish off from floodplain habitat that is important for salmon rearing. An eel-like fish, Pacific lamprey, was also supposed to benefit. If the barrier were removed, salmon and lamprey would have year-round access to the floodplain and the larger Gibbons Creek watershed. That was one of the main aims of the project.Taking the levee downConstruction began back in 2019, according to the Bonneville Power Administration, a US government agency that helped fund the work. More than two miles of the old levee were removed during summer 2021. The agency puts the exact length at 2.2 miles. The fish ladder where Gibbons Creek meets the Columbia River was taken out, and the creek was restored to its natural path. The Lower Columbia Estuary Partnership, which is one of the partners in the project, puts the cost of construction at $32 million. Bonneville’s own figure was $31 million, slightly below the partner estimate. The agency described the work as the largest habitat restoration project in the history of the lower Columbia River.Protecting nearby homes and businessesBringing down a levee doesn't mean leaving neighbours exposed. Crews built 1.6 miles of new setback levees, which are farther back from the river, according to the release. These protect the Port of Camas-Washougal Industrial Park, the city of Washougal’s wastewater treatment plant and private residents. A section of State Route 14 was also raised to the Columbia's 500-year flood level. The project pretty much eliminated the flood risk to the industrial park and significantly lowered operating costs, the Port's chief executive said in the release.What has changed so farThe project increased floodplain habitat for young salmon and steelhead between Bonneville Dam and the Willamette River by 19%. It also expanded habitat along the Pacific Flyway, a bird migration route from Alaska to Patagonia. Over 100 acres of wetlands were created, riparian habitat was restored within 250 acres, and more than 500,000 trees and shrubs, along with more than 14,000 pounds of native seeds, were planted. The refuge also added 1.1 miles of new trail. It was closed for two years during construction and reopened in May 2022. The extent to which these changes help the salmon population will only become clear over time. For now, Steigerwald shows how old infrastructure can be reimagined to consider a river, wildlife and nearby communities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2020 Kent, Washington closed Van Doren's Landing Park for a Green River levee project; in 2023 it reopened behind 1.4 miles of setback levee that cost $58 million
articles.summary: Van Doren’s Landing Park in Kent, Washington reopens after a major flood protection project, featuring a new 1.4-mile levee that enhances flood safety and restores vital fish habitats.
articles.body: The Van Doren's Landing Park has been one of the most preferred locations in Kent for many years due to its location next to the Green River Trail. This park is located near the Green River and poses a danger to nearby residents during flooding. In order to address this problem, Kent and King County embarked on a massive project of flood mitigation along this river. In July 2020, the city closed it to make way for a major flood protection project along the river, the Kent Reporter reported. Three years later, the park reopened after construction of a 1.4-mile setback levee, which moved the flood barrier far from the river and created more room for floodwater. According to the Salmon Recovery Portal, the work was part of the Lower Russell Levee Setback Project, a partnership involving the City of Kent and the King County Flood Control District. The project replaced an older levee and revetment that did not meet current engineering standards. The King County Flood Control District put the project cost at $58 million, a figure the Kent Reporter also used in its coverage of the 2023 grand opening.Why Kent needed to move the Green River levee The old levee was located near the eastern side of the Green River and between South 212th Street and South 228th Street, which was also called Veterans Drive. The new levee sits farther back from the river. This approach is known as a levee setback. Rather than hemming the river in, the barrier gives it room to spread out during floods. This provided the river with additional capacity for flooding and flow. According to King County’s project overview, the new levee replaced an older system that did not meet current design standards. The project also included a flood wall, riverbank improvements and changes to nearby roads and trails. According to King County's project page, the work was carried out in phases. The second phase, which began in 2020, included construction of the setback levee, habitat restoration and relocation of Van Doren’s Landing Park. This work required the park to close while construction was underway.The project restored habitat along the riverHabitat restoration was another key component of the project. Restoration also involved making improvements that benefit fish and wildlife along the Green River. According to the Washington Recreation and Conservation Office's project record, the restoration included construction of 15.8 acres of channel and off-channel habitat to the river. This provided juvenile salmon with habitat to search for food and cover. The same record lists another component of the project as the replanting of 24.3 acres of riparian habitat, which vegetated land on the edge of the river and the installation of large wood.The Washington Recreation and Conservation Office’s project record lists Chinook salmon and Green River steelhead among the threatened fish species associated with the restoration work. The improved habitat was intended to support these fish during their life cycles. The native plants found along the river also served as shade and supported the overall ecosystem. The combination of both the habitat restoration project and the levee setback was aimed at mitigating flooding concerns and enhancing the river itself.Van Doren’s Landing Park reopened in 2023The relocation of the Park took place during the second phase of the project, which also saw the construction of the levee and restoration of the habitat. Once that work was done, the park opened to the public. The project was completed in the spring of 2023. The park formally reopened at a grand opening ceremony on June 28, 2023, according to the Kent Reporter. The King County Flood Control District describes the completed Lower Russell Levee Setback Project as an investment in flood protection and the Green River corridor. The project was not just about the replacement of the levee, but also about updating the out-of-date system that protected from flooding, providing additional space during the high flow of water in the river and creating habitat for native fish species.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Bada bhai will be CM': Amit Shah after BJP-SAD announce alliance in Punjab
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on Tuesday sounded the poll bugle in Punjab, announcing an alliance for the 2027
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) on Tuesday sounded the poll bugle in Punjab, announcing an alliance for the 2027 assembly elections and reviving their partnership after a six-year break. The two parties will jointly contest all 117 seats, with the Akali Dal taking the lead in the alliance."Big brother will be Akali Dal. We will contest all 117 seats. Bada bhai hi chief minister hota hai (The elder brother becomes the chief minister)," Union home minister Amit Shah said at a joint press conference attended by BJP president Nitin Nabin and SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal.Also Read | 'Will make Punjab drug free by 2029': BJP-Akali Dal announce alliance on Gurpurab six years after split"Naturally, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) will play the role of the elder brother. The Akali Dal and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) will contest together. Both parties will jointly contest all 117 seats, while the Akali Dal will be in the role of the elder brother," he added.Shah said tackling drugs, corruption and law and order would be the alliance's key priorities in Punjab, a border state."The biggest hallmark of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) is that wherever there is an NDA government, law and order has remained sound. Both of our parties have discussed several issues concerning Punjab, and we have a consensus on them," he said.Also Read | 'Akali Dal-BJP alliance stood the test of time': PM Modi welcomes SAD's return to NDA"Our topmost priority will be a drug-free Punjab, fixing law and order to provide security in this border state, and eliminating these gangs. This is our topmost priority, and it will be the foremost issue in the manifestos of both parties," he added.Shah further stated that a detailed manifesto would be finalised soon by the two parties for the elections, but eradicating the drug menace from Punjab and promoting Hindu-Sikh unity would be among the key focus areas."BJP, the Akali Dal, and the NDA will contest in Punjab, and we will announce several key points in our manifesto. But, I want to make one thing very clear: eliminating drugs from Punjab will be our primary goal, eliminating corruption in Punjab will be our primary goal, and strengthening nationalist forces in Punjab will also be our primary goal. The current government in the state, led by Kejriwal Ji, had come to power promising to eliminate drugs within three months. They promised to eliminate drugs, but the problem has not been eradicated; it has increased. In 2017, Rahul Gandhi Ji had promised that drugs would be eliminated within one term. He made that promise, but his party also did nothing to address the drug problem. Now, I want to reiterate a promise that I made there: by December 31, 2029, we will make Punjab completely drug-free," he added.Sukhbir Singh Badal to be CM face: SirsaDelhi minister and BJP leader Manjinder Singh Sirsa said Sukhbir Singh Badal would be the chief ministerial face of the BJP-SAD alliance in Punjab.Speaking to ANI, Sirsa said the alliance was formed with a broader vision of addressing Punjab's problems rather than merely capturing political power. He said its priorities included making the state free of drugs, gangsters and debt, besides resolving farmers' issues.Also Read | ‘Zero plus zero equals zero’: AAP, Congress react to BJP-SAD alliance in PunjabHe also congratulated Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Shah, Nitin Nabin and Badal on the alliance, and welcomed the SAD's return to NDA.The announcement, made on Gurpurab, comes with a symbolic connection to the events that led to the breakdown of the alliance.The alliance marks a revival of ties between the BJP and SAD, which parted ways in 2020 after the Akali Dal withdrew from the NDA over its opposition to the now-repealed farm laws.Under their previous seat-sharing arrangement, the BJP contested 23 of Punjab's 117 assembly seats, while the SAD fought the remaining constituencies.The two parties had jointly governed Punjab for 10 years before losing the 2017 assembly elections. Congress returned to power under Captain Amarinder Singh.In 2022, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) swept the state, while the BJP and SAD, which contested separately, were pushed to the margins.Meanwhile, the Punjab BJP on Monday announced its 16-member state election committee for the 2027 assembly elections, with state president Kewal Singh Dhillon heading the panel.The committee comprises senior party leaders and former state presidents and has been tasked with preparing the party's electoral roadmap and framing a comprehensive chargesheet against the incumbent government.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A man buried in a sealed Egyptian pot 4,500 years ago carried a genetic surprise: about one-fifth of his ancestry was linked to Mesopotamia
articles.summary: Discover the surprising genetic ancestry of a 4,500-year-old man buried in Egypt, revealing a significant connection to ancient Mesopotamia and insights into cultural interactions in the ancient world.
articles.body: A man buried in a large ceramic pot in Egypt, more than 4,500 years ago, carried an unexpected genetic connection to the ancient Middle East. Scientists who analysed his DNA found that approximately 20% of his ancestry was linked to populations from the eastern Fertile Crescent, particularly ancient Mesopotamia. Most of his ancestry was associated with ancient North African populations. This breakthrough emerged from a paper that was released in the Journal Nature on July 2, 2025. The scientists analysed the genome of an adult male whose bones had been unearthed at the archaeological site called Nuwayrat, which is around 265 km south of Cairo. It is estimated through radiocarbon dating that he died between 2855 and 2570 BC, in the period when there was a transition from Egypt’s Early Dynastic Period to its Old Kingdom period. The discovery suggested that there existed ancestral relationships between ancient Egypt and the eastern Fertile Crescent. Moreover, the contact between these two regions entailed not just trade but also migration.A ceramic vessel helped preserve an ancient man’s remainsAccording to the Francis Crick Institute, the man's remains were discovered in 1902 during an excavation of a rock-cut tomb in Nuwayrat. The man had been buried within a large pottery jar, according to the Nature study. The study's authors noted that this kind of burial was often linked with people of high social status in the area. According to the Francis Crick Institute, the remains were first held at the Liverpool Institute of Archaeology, which later became part of the University of Liverpool and were then transferred to the World Museum Liverpool. It was through the tooth of the man that scientists obtained the genetic information needed for genome sequencing. Extraction of ancient DNA from Egypt was quite a challenge since the high temperatures accelerate the decay of DNA. In this case, the researchers proposed that the conditions in which the man had been buried may have been responsible for the preservation of the DNA. This method included the ceramic pot burial.The research was published under the title Whole-genome ancestry of an Old Kingdom Egyptian. It marked the first successful whole-genome sequencing of an individual from the early period of Egyptian dynastic history. The full study is available in the Journal Nature. The paper reports that the team sequenced the whole genome at 2× coverage from an adult male excavated at Nuwayrat, who lived a few centuries after Egypt's unification. Most of his ancestry was best matched to North African Neolithic populations, with additional signals linking him to the eastern Fertile Crescent, suggesting human movement, as well as cultural contact.One-fifth of his ancestry was linked to MesopotamiaIt was concluded that the majority of the ancestry of the man could be linked to Neolithic people of North Africa. About 20% ancestry was linked to the ancient population of the eastern Fertile Crescent, including Mesopotamia and other nearby regions. Mesopotamia covered large parts of modern-day Iraq. It was one of the places where cities and written languages were first formed. There were also contacts between ancient Egypt and the Fertile Crescent in general. These contacts included movements of people as well as of goods. Individuals with genetic ancestry related to ancient Mesopotamian populations might have migrated to Egypt and mixed there with native populations. However, scientists were unable to find out at which point in time this ancestry appeared and how many people brought it there.Chemical analysis of the man's teeth also provided additional information about him. It indicated that he was probably born in Egypt and grew up there. Thus, the genetics linked to Mesopotamia cannot be evidence of personal migration from modern-day Iraq. Instead, his ancestry reflected connections between populations that had developed over generations. The research also compared his genome with DNA from other ancient populations to estimate where his ancestry came from. Their findings were based on the available reference samples, so future discoveries could refine the picture.His bones offered clues about his possible occupationThe bones of the man revealed more facts about his way of life. Some indications of continuous physical activities were found in the form of enlargement of muscle insertions, modifications in his arms and arthritis in the right foot. All these findings indicated several years of hard physical labour. The researchers believed that pottery making could be his profession since movements involved in operating a pottery wheel can account for these skeletal modifications.However, they could not prove that he was a potter, as other kinds of activities involving similar movements might also result in these modifications. Another mystery arose due to his burial. The presence of ceramic vessels along with a rock-cut tomb was indicative of the fact that this individual enjoyed some kind of treatment usually given to people of high social status, but this was not expected considering the findings from the skeleton, which indicated that he performed hard labour. However, one person’s genome cannot represent the entire population of ancient Egypt. The researchers stressed that more DNA samples from different regions and periods were needed to understand how ancestry varied across the country and how populations changed over time.You use AI every day. articles.title: Read Amazon's notice to its customers in New York telling them: Go to your City Council and ask them to …
articles.summary: Amazon has started asking its New York City customers to oppose a proposed bill that could change how the company handles deliveries.
articles.body: Amazon has started asking its New York City customers to oppose a proposed bill that could change how the company handles deliveries. The company has displayed a warning on its app and website saying: “NYC Council Could add up to $5 per order.” The notice refers to the Delivery Protection Act, a bill backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani that proposes new safety, training and employment rules for delivery operators. Amazon says the proposed rules could increase delivery costs and is urging customers to contact their City Council members before the bill is passed.What does Amazon's notice to New York customers sayAmazon's notice links customers to an online form where they can enter their name and address. The form then prepares an email to their local City Council member asking them to oppose the bill. The drafted message reads: “As your constituent, I am writing to urge you to oppose Intro 518, a bill that threatens to raise costs for New Yorkers like me,”It further claims: “This bill could increase my annual delivery costs by up to $664 per year. In a city already facing an affordability crisis, that’s money I cannot afford to lose—and neither can my neighbors.”Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said: “As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written—which is why we’re doing this,”She added: “If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill. ”Amazon said customers sent around 60,000 emails to council members in the first 36 hours of the campaign.What is the Delivery Protection ActThe Delivery Protection Act, introduced by City Councilmember Tiffany Cabán and backed by Mamdani, would require warehouse operators such as Amazon to obtain city licences and meet new safety, training and employment requirements. It would also require Amazon to directly hire couriers who currently work for smaller companies that deliver its packages.What Zohran Mamdani said about Amazon's warningZohran Mamdani criticised Amazon's campaign in a post on X, writing: “Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company,” He added: “If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council’s efforts to protect workers’ rights and keep our streets safe. articles.title: Around 25,000 bank employees to strike on Dec 3 over proposed IDBI Bank sale to Canadian firm Fairfax, likely disrupting 3,700 branches and transactions worth Rs 1,200 crore in Gujarat
articles.summary: AHMEDABAD: Banking operations across Gujarat are likely to be disrupted on December 3 as around 25,000 bank employees and officers are expected to
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: Banking operations across Gujarat are likely to be disrupted on December 3 as around 25,000 bank employees and officers are expected to participate in a nationwide strike against the proposed sale of IDBI Bank to Canadian financial services firm Fairfax Financial Holdings.The strike could affect nearly 3,700 bank branches across Gujarat and disrupt transactions worth around Rs 1,200 crore, according to the Maha Gujarat Bank Employees’ Association (MGBEA).In a strike notice served on IDBI Bank MD and CEO, the UFIOE said the strike would be observed across all branches and offices of the bank nationwide.The All India Bank Employees’ Association (AIBEA), All India Bank Officers’ Association (AIBOA) and Bank Employees Federation of India (BEFI) have called for a solidarity strike in support of IDBI Bank employees and officers.The decision comes despite the government's assurance that the service conditions and pension benefits of existing employees will remain protected after the transaction.The All India Bank Employees' Association (AIBEA), All India Bank Officers Association (AIBOA) and Bank Employees Federation of India (BEFI) have called for a solidarity strike in support of IDBI Bank employees and officers protesting the proposed transfer of control to a foreign investor.The unions termed the proposed sale unwarranted, arguing that public sector banks play a crucial role in safeguarding people's savings. They said IDBI Bank has deposits of around Rs 3.5 lakh crore and advances of Rs 2.5 lakh crore, taking its total business to approximately Rs 6 lakh crore.The December 3 strike comes after IDBI Bank employees and officers staged a two-day protest on November 2 and 3. The unions said the government had continued with the proposed sale despite the earlier agitation.The Union Cabinet approved the sale of a 60.72 per cent stake in IDBI Bank to a subsidiary of Fairfax Financial Holdings on October 14 for Rs 52,878 crore.As part of the proposed transaction, the government will divest its 30.48 per cent stake in the bank, while the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) will sell its 30.24 per cent holding. Following the transaction, the government's stake will come down to 15 per cent and LIC's shareholding to 19 per cent.However, DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla said in October that the share purchase agreement would safeguard the service conditions of existing employees and their pension benefits. He also said a separate pension fund had been set up for existing pensioners and would be fully maintained."Existing employees and existing pensioners should have no apprehensions, as their service conditions have been fully protected," Chawla had said.The proposed disinvestment has also faced criticism from Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, who warned that privatisation could end reservation protections for SC, ST and OBC candidates. He also questioned the move despite IDBI Bank reporting a profit of over Rs 9,000 crore last year.The unions have also flagged concerns over the banking sector's handling of bad loans. They alleged that private corporate borrowers were responsible for large non-performing loans and that banks had incurred losses through loan write-offs.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ahmedabad | Silver Rate in Ahmedabad | Bank Holidays in Ahmedabad | Public Holidays in Ahmedabad | Ahmedabad AQI | Weather in Ahmedabad | Petrol Price in Ahmedabad | Diesel Price in Ahmedabad | CNG Price in Ahmedabad | LPG Price in AhmedabadStay updated with the latest Ahmedabad news. articles.title: Los Angeles couple Andrew and Brigid Elrod won $7.65 million after a jury heard their Koreatown landlord's former manager say the boss suggested staff wear fake ICE uniforms to scare Latino tenants out
articles.summary: A Los Angeles couple have been awarded $7.65 million after winning a legal battle against the company that owned their former apartment building in
articles.body: A Los Angeles couple have been awarded $7.65 million after winning a legal battle against the company that owned their former apartment building in Koreatown. The case involved allegations that the landlord used intimidation, rent increases and poor living conditions to push residents out of their homes.Andrew and Brigid Elrod took legal action against K3 Holdings after becoming involved in efforts to organise tenants living in the building. According to LA Times, they alleged that the company retaliated against residents who challenged its practices and wanted tenants paying lower rents to leave so that the apartments could be rented at higher rates.The case took a significant turn during the trial when a former employee of K3 Holdings gave evidence about a suggestion allegedly made by the company's principal, Nathan Kadisha. According to the former asset manager, Kadisha had proposed that employees wear fake Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) uniforms to frighten Latino tenants into leaving a building. The former employee also testified that Kadisha did not want African Americans to rent the company's properties.The jury ultimately found the landlord responsible for harassing and retaliating against the Elrods. It also found that the company had failed to maintain the apartment building properly. The couple received $4.5 million for the impact of their experience, including anxiety, humiliation, grief, inconvenience and emotional distress. A further $3.15 million was awarded as punitive damages against K3 Holdings and three related companies.The decision was delivered on Friday by a Los Angeles Superior Court jury. It was an 11-1 verdict, bringing the couple's case to a successful conclusion after they chose to continue with the lawsuit while several other tenants reached settlements.Tenants challenged property managementThe Elrods' involvement in the dispute dates back to 2021, when a limited liability corporation controlled by K3 Holdings purchased their apartment building at 974 S. Gramercy Place in Koreatown.After the acquisition, the couple joined other residents in setting up a tenants' association. They also became active in the K3 Tenant Council, which was affiliated with the Los Angeles Tenants Union.Their organising activities were followed by a confrontation with the landlord over construction work at the property. The residents raised concerns about what they described as illegal and unsafe construction practices. The Elrods later took part in a sit-in protest against the work.Rose Lenehan, an organiser with the Tenants Union, said the couple were served eviction notices after participating in the protest. They continued to face eviction threats and eventually left the apartment in 2023.The couple alleged that these actions were part of a wider effort to remove tenants who were paying rents below the prevailing market rates. According to their claims, K3 Holdings used maintenance problems, construction activities and intimidation to encourage residents to accept buyout offers and vacate their homes.The company's property portfolio included 39 buildings. However, the jury's verdict in the Elrods' case concerned only the Koreatown property.Emails and messages presented during trialThe jury also considered communications involving Kadisha during the proceedings. These included text messages and emails that formed part of the evidence against the property company.One message discussed how construction-related displacement could help the company persuade tenants to accept financial offers to leave.In the message, Kadisha told a colleague that forcing tenants to relocate during construction would "be a very strong case to take the buyout", according to a statement on the verdict issued by the Los Angeles Tenants Union.The jury examined the company's treatment of residents in detail. Its 30-page verdict included findings on several questions relating to the landlord's conduct.It found that K3 Holdings and its subsidiaries had raised rents and reduced utility services as ways of putting pressure on tenants to move out. The jury also concluded that the companies had engaged in conduct covered by Los Angeles' 2021 Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance.Jacob Woocher, one of the lawyers representing the Elrods, said the evidence was not limited to the couple's individual experience.He said the trial had presented material about the company's practices across several properties, even though the verdict itself covered only the building where the couple had lived.Other tenants settled, but Elrods continued lawsuitThe Elrods were among several tenants involved in a 2022 lawsuit against K3 Holdings. According to Lenehan, a number of the other residents eventually settled their claims.The couple decided to continue pursuing their case instead. Their legal team included the Los Angeles Center for Community Law and Action and Alfredo Nava of the Law Office of Alfredo Nava.Their decision meant that the allegations were examined in a trial, where the jury heard testimony from a former company employee and considered internal communications and other evidence.The final award included both compensation for the harm suffered by the couple and punitive damages against the companies. The $4.5 million in non-economic damages covered the past and future impact of the alleged harassment, while the additional $3.15 million was imposed as punishment.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Chor hai tera chacha’: When Priyanka Gandhi slapped a boy in school over Emergency taunts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The 1977 election defeat followed the Gandhi family into childhood, Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi recalled, sharing memories of school taunts and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The 1977 election defeat followed the Gandhi family into childhood, Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi recalled, sharing memories of school taunts and tense days at home in a candid conversation with their mother Sonia Gandhi, released in a video on Tuesday.In the video titled ‘What Ma Left Out of Her Book’, the siblings looked back at the days after their grandmother Indira Gandhi and uncle Sanjay lost the election following the Emergency, when the family moved to a different house and, as Priyanka put it, “there was a lot of tension in the air”.The conversation turned to their first day back at school after the electoral defeat. Priyanka recalled a boy approaching her with a taunt about Sanjay, who had been jailed in connection with the ‘Kissa Kursi Ka’ case.“I remember a little boy coming and telling me, ‘Tera chacha jail mein hai; chor hai tera chacha’,” she said. “So I gave him a slap and he started crying. We went to the teacher and I got a scolding.”The siblings’ recollections offered a glimpse of how the political upheaval of the Emergency years spilled into the everyday lives of Indira Gandhi’s grandchildren.Rahul, meanwhile, remembered a different kind of isolation at school. He said that when he sat down on the first day after the election, no one took the seat next to him. He did not say anything, but recalled that classmates were not talking to him and were being “a bit mean”.Sonia Gandhi interjected as Rahul spoke about the remarks children had made about their grandmother. The family also recalled a birthday party that Priyanka had arranged in an attempt to mend things. She had invited 32 children, but 15 minutes after the scheduled time, nobody had arrived. Eventually, only one friend turned up — a friend Rahul said he still has.The conversation also brought out the contrasting personalities of the two siblings. Priyanka said she had been a prefect and was suited to the school system, while Rahul described himself as rebellious, always asking questions and disturbing things.“She wasn’t rebellious. She always followed the rules,” Rahul said of Priyanka. “And I was rebellious, always asking questions.”Priyanka joked that the same difference could be seen in Parliament today, saying she was suited to the system while Rahul was not.The memories come days after the launch of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, which recounts episodes from her family life and the Emergency period.The 1977 election was the only electoral defeat for Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi. It followed the Emergency, imposed from June 1975 to March 1977, during which civil liberties were curtailed and political opponents were jailed.Sanjay Gandhi was convicted in the ‘Kissa Kursi Ka’ case in February 1979, along with former information and broadcasting minister V C Shukla, over charges related to the destruction of prints of the satirical film. The conviction was later overturned on appeal.Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi returned to electoral victory in 1980. Sanjay died in an air crash in 1981, after which Rajiv Gandhi entered politics and won the Amethi seat. He held it until his assassination during the 1991 election campaign.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: California prepares for flooding, heavy rain and strong winds before Thanksgiving as king tides and mountain snow threaten holiday travel across the West Coast
articles.summary: California is preparing for another round of heavy rain, flooding and strong winds as storms move towards the state during one of the busiest travel
articles.body: California is preparing for another round of heavy rain, flooding and strong winds as storms move towards the state during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. A Pacific storm is expected to reach Northern California on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing an atmospheric river, persistent rainfall and potentially hazardous travel conditions. The threat comes at the same time as the year's highest tides, raising the risk of coastal flooding across the San Francisco Bay Area. Officials have moved emergency resources into position, while forecasters warn that rain, wind, snow and high surf could complicate Thanksgiving travel.California faces heavy rain, flooding and strong winds during Thanksgiving weekThe latest storm system is expected to reach the Northern California coast on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing moisture from the Pacific in the form of an atmospheric river. According to NBC News, the National Weather Service's San Francisco Bay Area office forecast widespread and persistent rain, with up to 3 inches possible in northern parts of the region.The rain is expected to arrive alongside strong winds. Gusts of up to 45 mph are possible in parts of the Bay Area, while the combination of heavy rainfall, runoff and high tides could increase the risk of flooding in low-lying areas. A coastal flood warning covering the Bay Area coastline is in effect from Monday morning through Thursday afternoon, with nearly 3 feet of inundation possible in vulnerable locations.The weather threat is not limited to rainfall. The first storm is expected to bring fresh snow to higher elevations of the Sierra Nevada, potentially creating difficult driving conditions during the Thanksgiving travel rush. The National Weather Service office in Reno warned that the snow could produce periods of difficult travel during an already busy holiday period.A second storm containing atmospheric river precipitation is also expected to follow the first system. Forecasters said there was considerable uncertainty about the second storm's exact timing, location and strength, with another round of unsettled weather potentially arriving later in the week.King tides could worsen coastal flooding across San Francisco BayThe storm threat is particularly concerning because it coincides with king tides, the highest tides of the year. The California Coastal Commission said the king tides are expected from Tuesday through Thursday, meaning heavy rain and storm runoff could reach waterways at the same time as exceptionally high tides.The ABC News report said the National Weather Service warned that high tides could cause flooding of low-lying infrastructure, road closures and coastal erosion. Wednesday morning's high tide could approach the highest level on record in San Francisco, with the full moon, elevated surf and El Niño conditions contributing to unusually high water levels.King tides across the Bay Area could reach 7.5 to 8 feet above the average low tide, according to the US Coast Guard. Water levels could rise 1 to 2 feet above normal high tides and potentially higher if the peak tides coincide with an incoming storm. Coastal and low-lying areas around San Francisco Bay, San Pablo Bay, Marin County, San Mateo County and the San Francisco waterfront are among the areas vulnerable to temporary flooding and closures.The combination of storm runoff and high tides has already prompted preparations in San Francisco. Mayor Daniel Lurie said the city's emergency operations centre was being activated ahead of the expected rain and tide-driven flooding. He also urged residents to consider staying home rather than travelling during the most hazardous part of the week.Thanksgiving travel faces possible road closures and dangerous conditionsThe timing of the storms could make the weather particularly disruptive because Tuesday and Wednesday are expected to be among the busiest road travel days before Thanksgiving. Heavy rain, coastal flooding, strong winds and mountain snow could affect roads at the same time as millions of people begin travelling for the holiday.According to ABC News, AAA estimates that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday and the following Monday. The weather threat therefore comes during a period when California roads and airports are expected to be under heavy demand.The California Governor's Office of Emergency Services has moved resources, including swift-water rescue teams, to areas where they may be needed because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding. The state is preparing for the possibility that rising water could affect roads and other infrastructure during the holiday period.Some transportation precautions have already been announced. California Department of Transportation officials said the Posey Tube, an East Bay tunnel connecting Alameda Island with Oakland beneath the Oakland Estuary, would be closed as a precaution from Sunday through Friday. Other coastal roads and low-lying routes could also face temporary closures if flooding develops.Northern and Southern California could both see coastal floodingNorthern California is expected to experience the strongest impacts from the first storm, but coastal flooding concerns extend farther south. The National Weather Service has issued a coastal flood advisory covering parts of the Southern California coast, including Catalina and Santa Barbara islands and sections of Santa Barbara County.ABC News reported that the first storm was expected to bring lighter rain to San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties, while significant rainfall was less likely to reach urban Los Angeles. Even so, high tides and elevated surf could create flooding concerns along exposed coastal areas.The Port of San Diego also planned to close two public-access trails along San Diego Bay for the week because of king tide concerns. The precautions reflect a broader West Coast threat, with coastal flood alerts and high-surf advisories covering large sections of the Pacific coastline.The unsettled pattern is expected to continue beyond the first storm. Forecasters are tracking another system that could affect the West Coast later in the week, although its precise timing and strength remain uncertain. For California residents and Thanksgiving travellers, the combination of heavy rain, strong winds, high tides and mountain snow means conditions could change quickly during one of the country's busiest travel periods.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ex-Russian president warns Ukraine of nuclear strike: What options does Moscow have
articles.summary: Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev is back with another chilling nuclear warning, this time spelling out the circumstances that could push Moscow
articles.body: Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev is back with another chilling nuclear warning, this time spelling out the circumstances that could push Moscow towards using atomic weapons in the Ukraine war.Medvedev has warned that massive conventional attacks capable of causing catastrophic damage could make a preventive nuclear strike by Russia possible, raising the stakes for Ukraine and its western allies.Going a step further, he has argued that covert western supplies of nuclear weapons to Kyiv would also justify such an attack, claiming that Russia has not only the right but, under certain circumstances, the obligation to use its nuclear arsenal.According to Russian state news agency TASS, Medvedev argued that the large-scale use of conventional weapons capable of causing man-made, environmental or social catastrophes could bring a preventive nuclear strike into consideration."The foundations of state policy effectively provide for a pre-emptive nuclear strike if the very existence of our state is threatened or our country has sustained unacceptable damage," he wrote in the article published in the Moscow Journal of International Law.He further claimed that Ukraine, Nato members and other western countries had already created situations in which Moscow could consider using its nuclear arsenal.In his strongest warning, Medvedev said Kyiv and its western supporters must understand that Russia could be compelled to cross the nuclear threshold under certain circumstances."Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.However, Medvedev acknowledged that Moscow had not yet considered nuclear weapons necessary in the nearly five-year war against Ukraine."Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote, adding that the decision rested with President Vladimir Putin.He said Putin would make such a decision after a comprehensive assessment of the circumstances, weighing the actual damage inflicted on Russia against the proportionality of any retaliatory measures.Russia lowered its nuclear threshold in 2024Medvedev's latest warning comes against the backdrop of Russia's decision to expand the circumstances under which it could consider using nuclear weapons.In November 2024, President Vladimir Putin approved a revised nuclear doctrine, lowering the threshold for a potential nuclear strike and broadening the range of conventional attacks that could trigger such a response.The move came days after the Joe Biden administration authorised Ukraine to use US-supplied long-range ATACMS missiles against certain targets inside Russian territory, a decision Moscow had repeatedly warned could escalate the conflict.The revised doctrine identifies five circumstances in which Russia could consider using its nuclear arsenal.The revised doctrine identifies five circumstances in which Russia could consider using nuclear weapons. These include reliable information about an incoming ballistic missile attack. The use of nuclear or other weapons of mass destruction against Russia or its allies is another trigger.Moscow could also consider nuclear use if an attack targets critical government or military facilities and threatens its ability to retaliate with nuclear weapons. The doctrine further includes conventional aggression posing a critical threat to the sovereignty or territorial integrity of Russia or Belarus.The fifth condition covers reliable information about a mass launch of aircraft, cruise missiles, drones or hypersonic weapons crossing Russia's borders.What nuclear options does Russia have against UkraineRussia possesses one of the world's largest nuclear arsenals, including both tactical and strategic nuclear weapons.According to the UK Parliament's House of Commons Library, Moscow had an estimated stockpile of around 1,558 non-strategic nuclear warheads in its December 2024 assessment. These weapons are designed primarily for regional military scenarios and could potentially be used in a conflict such as the war in Ukraine. However, the estimate does not mean all these warheads are deployed or immediately available for use.Among Russia's key nuclear-capable delivery systems is the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile, which can carry either conventional or nuclear warheads.Russia also has nuclear-capable aircraft, including the Tu-22M3 bomber and Su-34 fighter-bomber, alongside cruise missile systems such as nuclear-capable variants of the Kalibr and 9M729. These platforms provide Moscow with multiple delivery options, although their conventional use in Ukraine does not indicate that nuclear warheads are involved.Beyond tactical weapons, Russia maintains a strategic nuclear triad comprising land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and nuclear-capable strategic bombers.These weapons are primarily intended to deter or conduct nuclear operations against major adversaries. Their use against Ukraine would represent a far more extreme escalation, with potentially devastating consequences for European and global security.A limited tactical nuclear strike could trigger a much wider international confrontation, forcing the United States and Nato to consider their response while increasing the risk of further escalation.Although Moscow could theoretically use a nuclear demonstration or battlefield nuclear weapon to pressure Kyiv and its western supporters, such a move would carry enormous military, diplomatic and economic consequences.You use AI every day.
